name: Basque Chicken and Peppers (Pollo al Chilindron)

prose.intro_html: Chilindron is the Spanish name for what happens when red peppers, onions, tomato, and a little smoked paprika cook down around browned chicken until the whole pot tastes like far more than the sum of its parts. Bone-in, skin-on thighs and drumsticks earn their place here because the skin browns into flavor and the bones keep the meat from drying out over a slow simmer. A handful of diced bacon does the job Spanish cooks give to jamon, and a splash of dry white wine lifts every browned bit off the bottom of the pot. Built at 14 servings it runs about {{cal}} calories and {{protein}} grams of protein a serving, with under 10 grams of carbs. That is a Sunday-in-Spain dinner on a Tuesday budget.
shop_smart: Bone-in, skin-on chicken is the whole plate. You want about four and two-thirds pounds of thighs, drumsticks, or a mix of both. Buy it bone-in and skin-on on purpose, because the skin browns into flavor and the bones keep the meat juicy through the braise. The big family pack is the cheapest way to buy chicken.

Red peppers and onions build the base. Roughly four and a half red bell peppers and a couple of onions, all sliced thin. This is where chilindron gets its color and its sweetness, so this is not the place to cut corners.

A few ounces of bacon do the jamon's job. About eight ounces of diced bacon carries the smoky, salty backbone that Spanish cooks pull from jamon Serrano. Bacon is the recipe's own listed stand-in and it is on every shelf in town.

Canned fire-roasted tomatoes are the sauce. You need a little over two cans of fire-roasted diced tomatoes. The fire-roasting is worth reaching for because the char is already built in, but plain diced tomatoes will do if that is what is in the pantry.

Dry white wine and smoked paprika make it Spanish. Just about a cup of any dry white you would actually drink, plus smoked Spanish paprika, sometimes labeled pimenton. Skip the bottle marked cooking wine and reach for the real thing.
Garlic, bay, fresh thyme, a spoon of sugar, and olive oil round it out. These are pantry and produce backbone you most likely already have on hand, so they barely move the cart.
make_it: Weigh your empty Dutch oven or deep skillet and write the number down. You will use it at the end to split this into 14 even servings by weight instead of eyeballing every container.
Pat the chicken pieces dry with paper towels and season them all over with the kosher salt and black pepper.

Heat the olive oil in the pot over medium-high heat. Working in batches so the pot is not crowded, sear the chicken skin-side down until golden, about 3 to 4 minutes a side. It will not be cooked through yet. Move it to a plate.
Reduce the heat to medium. Add the sliced onion, red bell peppers, diced bacon, and garlic. Cook, stirring now and then, until the onion turns translucent, 8 to 10 minutes.
Stir in the smoked paprika and cook about 30 seconds, just until it smells toasty.
Add the fire-roasted tomatoes, white wine, sugar, bay leaves, and fresh thyme. Scrape the bottom of the pot to loosen every browned bit into the sauce.

Nestle the chicken back into the sauce along with any collected juices. Bring it to a boil, then drop the heat to low and hold a gentle simmer, uncovered, about 35 minutes, until the chicken is tender and reads 190 to 195 degrees F at the bone.

Fish out the bay leaves and thyme stems. Weigh the full pot and subtract the empty weight from Step 1 to get the cooked total. Divide by 14 and give each container an even share of chicken and pepper-tomato sauce, aiming for that weight.
prose.portion_html: Set the full pot on your scale and subtract the empty weight you wrote down in Step 1 to get the cooked total. Divide that number by 14. Each container gets an even share of chicken and pepper-tomato sauce, landing near {{cal}} calories with {{protein}} grams of protein.
prose.cost_closing_html: About ${{cost_ps}} a serving (at everyday cost) for a Spanish braise that tastes like it simmered all afternoon. The chicken and the peppers carry it; the bacon and the wine just make it taste expensive.

head.description: Basque chicken chilindron for meal prep: bone-in skin-on chicken braised with red peppers, onions, bacon, fire-roasted tomatoes, white wine, and smoked paprika, built for 14 servings. About {{cal}} calories and {{protein}} grams of protein per serving, with under 10 grams of carbs.
head.keywords: basque chicken, pollo al chilindron, spanish chicken and peppers, low carb meal prep, high protein chicken dinner
steps: Pat the chicken dry and season it with the kosher salt and black pepper.
Sear the chicken skin-side down in olive oil until golden but not cooked through, then set it aside.
Cook the onion, red peppers, bacon, and garlic until the onion is translucent, then bloom the smoked paprika.
Add the fire-roasted tomatoes, white wine, sugar, bay, and thyme, nestle the chicken back in, and simmer to 190 degrees F.
Weigh the pot, subtract the empty weight, and divide across 14 containers.
